name: Assyrian Empire

fields.foundation: The Assyrian Empire began in the city of Assur on the west bank of the Tigris in northern Mesopotamia, which became an independent city-state around 2025 BCE after the collapse of the Third Dynasty of Ur. Puzur-Ashur I founded a dynasty that gave continuity to later Assyrian kingship. In the early centuries Assyrian power was commercial rather than military. It rested on a network of Assyrian merchant colonies in Anatolia, of which the karum at Kanesh (modern Kültepe in Turkey) was the most important. More than 20,000 cuneiform tablets from Kanesh document Assyrian merchants bringing tin from the east, probably from Iran and Central Asia, and textiles from Babylonia and Assur itself, and exchanging them for Anatolian silver and gold. Modern estimates suggest that around 100 tons of tin and some 100,000 textiles passed through the network over the half-century best covered by the archives. This was a commercial empire, not a territorial one: its power came from trade relationships rather than garrisons. Territorial ambition first appeared under the Amorite conqueror Shamshi-Adad I (r. c. 1808–1776 BCE), who seized Assur, styled himself "King of the Universe" and built a kingdom of Upper Mesopotamia stretching from the Zagros foothills to the Euphrates and Mari. This kingdom fell apart soon after his death. A long period of weakness followed, ending in subjection to Mitanni. The Middle Assyrian kingdom then emerged under Ashur-uballit I (r. c. 1365–1330 BCE), who used the Hittite defeat of Mitanni to assert independence and claim equality with the great kings of Egypt and Babylon. The empire's greatest phase was the Neo-Assyrian revival, which began in 911 BCE under Adad-nirari II and culminated in Esarhaddon's conquest of Egypt in 671 BCE, when Assyria became the largest empire the world had yet seen.
fields.socioeconomy: The Assyrian economy changed fundamentally over a history of some fourteen centuries, from the commercial network of the Old Assyrian period to the tribute system of the Neo-Assyrian Empire. Thousands of business tablets from Kanesh record the contracts, loans, partnerships and family correspondence of the early period. They are among the earliest evidence of organised long-distance private enterprise in world history: merchants worked under a legal framework that protected contracts and settled disputes through the city assembly of Assur and the colonies' own councils. In the Middle and Neo-Assyrian periods the economy turned towards extracting agricultural surplus and tribute from conquered peoples. The empire's systematic deportation policy moved whole communities from conquered territories to the Assyrian heartland and to under-populated provinces, which broke potential resistance and supplied agricultural and craft labour where the state needed it. At its peak the Neo-Assyrian economy channelled the agricultural surpluses of Mesopotamia, the timber of Lebanon, the metals of Anatolia, the horses of the Zagros and the luxury goods of Phoenician trade into the construction of enormous royal cities at Nimrud, Khorsabad and Nineveh. From the 740s BCE the reforms of Tiglath-pileser III broke up large provinces and turned many vassal states into directly administered territories. They greatly increased the flow of revenue to the centre and paid for the campaigns that carried the empire to its greatest extent. The Library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh, whose remains comprise some 30,000 tablets and fragments, shows that learning as well as wealth was concentrated at the imperial centre.
fields.military: The Assyrian army was the strongest and most systematically organised fighting force of its age, and its innovations in tactics, logistics, siege warfare and intelligence influenced warfare in the Near East for centuries. The Neo-Assyrian army as reorganised under Tiglath-pileser III (r. 745–727 BCE) combined a standing professional core, the kisir sharruti or king's cohort, with provincial levies and allied contingents. It was organised into specialised units of chariotry, cavalry, infantry, engineers and siege troops, and equipped on a large scale with iron weapons. Assyrian siege warfare was without precedent. Engineers used wheeled battering rams, siege towers, ramps and mining to reduce heavily fortified cities, as the reliefs of Sennacherib's siege of Lachish in 701 BCE record. The empire's reputation for systematic brutality against populations that resisted was a deliberate psychological weapon, meant to encourage surrender. A network of royal roads, relay stations and informants allowed the king to coordinate operations across an empire spanning thousands of kilometres with a speed unmatched by earlier states. Its military achievements included Tukulti-Ninurta I's conquest of Babylon (c. 1225 BCE) and capture of the Kassite king Kashtiliash IV, which made him the first Assyrian king to rule Babylon, and Esarhaddon's conquest of Egypt in 671 BCE, which made the Neo-Assyrian Empire the largest the world had yet seen. Ashurbanipal's destruction of the Elamite capital Susa around 647 BCE, at the end of a devastating war that ended Elam as a major power, showed that the army could wage a war of annihilation. It failed at last against the Medo-Babylonian coalition of the 610s BCE, when the combined forces of Cyaxares the Mede and Nabopolassar of Babylon overwhelmed even Assyria's fortified heartland.
fields.governance: Assyrian government developed over a millennium and a half. Old Assyrian Assur was an oligarchic city-state with a city assembly, an annual eponym official (limmu) chosen by lot, and a council of elders; under the Neo-Assyrian kings it had become the most developed territorial administration the ancient world had yet produced. The provincial system, most fully elaborated by Tiglath-pileser III from the 740s BCE, divided the empire into provinces under appointed governors answerable directly to the king. Many of them were eunuchs without dynastic ambitions, which curbed the power of hereditary magnates who might develop independent ambitions. A relay system of royal couriers, supplemented by fire signals, connected provincial governors to the palace so quickly that the king could respond to threats within days rather than weeks, and thousands of surviving letters attest to the intensity of this correspondence. Mass deportation was an administrative strategy as well as a punishment: it broke the kinship networks that sustained resistance, mixed populations in ways that weakened local identities, and supplied labour where the empire needed it most. Royal ideology was carefully constructed through monumental art and inscription. Palace reliefs depicting the king in battle, the hunt and ritual, such as the celebrated lion hunt reliefs of Ashurbanipal now in the British Museum, proclaimed royal power as at once military, cosmic and divinely sanctioned, the king acting as the earthly agent of the god Ashur. Ashurbanipal's library at Nineveh was built up by systematically collecting and copying texts from across Mesopotamia. The state sought to control territory and tribute, and also the entire scholarly heritage of Mesopotamian civilisation.
fields.impact: The Assyrian Empire affected later civilisation in several ways, through the administrative and military models it established and the cultural mixing it forced through deportation and conquest. Neo-Assyrian practices, including provincial government, relay communications, intelligence networks and the use of Aramaic alongside Akkadian in administration, were inherited by the Neo-Babylonian Empire and then by the Achaemenid Persians, who built consciously on Mesopotamian imperial precedent. Tiglath-pileser III's deportations from Galilee in 732 BCE and the fall of Samaria in 722 BCE, followed by Sargon II's deportation of the population of the Kingdom of Israel, the "Ten Lost Tribes" of biblical tradition, marked the history of Israel and Judah deeply; the Assyrian crisis is reflected in the prophetic books of Isaiah, Hosea and Micah, and in the biblical account of Sennacherib's siege of Jerusalem in 701 BCE. The Library of Ashurbanipal, rediscovered at Nineveh by Austen Henry Layard and Hormuzd Rassam in the mid-nineteenth century, preserved the standard version of the Epic of Gilgamesh, one of the oldest surviving works of literature, along with thousands of texts on Mesopotamian divination, medicine and religion that might otherwise have been lost. Assyrian siege techniques and military organisation were adopted in turn by the Babylonians and Persians, as part of a continuous tradition of military engineering that extended to the Hellenistic world. Assyria's documented brutality, cities razed, populations deported and enemies impaled as shown in palace reliefs, gave it a fearsome reputation that stayed in Near Eastern political memory for generations and established deterrence through publicised atrocity as a deliberate instrument of imperial rule.
fields.decline: The collapse of the Neo-Assyrian Empire is among the most debated events of antiquity. A state that had stood at the apex of world power in 671 BCE was annihilated within little more than sixty years, its capital cities destroyed and its ruling class extinguished so thoroughly that no Assyrian successor state emerged. Several causes reinforced one another. Ashurbanipal's long reign (669–c. 631 BCE) left an empire at its greatest extent but overstretched, and the final decades of his rule are so poorly documented that even the date of his death is uncertain. The empire had also accumulated enemies with strong motives for revenge among the peoples it had conquered: Babylonians who remembered Sennacherib's sacrilegious destruction of their city in 689 BCE, Elamites whose kingdom had been devastated, and the Israelites and other deported populations of the Levant. The civil war of 652–648 BCE between Ashurbanipal and his brother Shamash-shum-ukin, king of Babylon, had already shown how fragile Assyrian control was in the south. The succession disputes that followed Ashurbanipal's death gave an opening to Nabopolassar, traditionally regarded as a Chaldean chieftain, who seized Babylon in 626 BCE and declared independence. His alliance with Cyaxares of Media produced a coalition too strong to be resisted. The Medes sacked Assur in 614 BCE, the Babylonians and Medes together destroyed Nineveh in 612 BCE, and the last Assyrian king, Ashur-uballit II, abandoned his refuge at Harran in 610 BCE and, after the fall of Harran, failed with Egyptian help to retake it in 609. He then disappears from the historical record without a documented death. The empire's great cities lay buried until archaeologists uncovered them in the nineteenth century.
fields.summary: The Assyrian Empire made systematic terror an instrument of imperial rule. It also assembled the first great systematically collected library, preserved the Epic of Gilgamesh for posterity, and established the provincial administration and record-keeping on which the empires of the ancient Near East were built.
fields.teaser: The Neo-Assyrian Empire became the most feared military power of its age, perfecting siege warfare and using terror as a deliberate tool of rule. At its height it stretched from Egypt to western Iran.
fields.t0: From the city of Assur on the Tigris, Assyria grew from a merchant network into the largest empire the world had yet seen.
fields.t1: Its provinces, royal couriers, siege engineers and mass deportations became models for Babylon and Persia.
fields.t2: Overstretched and hated by its subjects, it was destroyed by Medes and Babylonians in barely sixty years after its peak.
fields.dyk: The Library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh preserved the standard version of the Epic of Gilgamesh, one of the oldest surviving works of literature.
